topics.title: GDB
topics.description: GNU Debugger: breakpoints, watchpoints, core dumps, threads and remote debugging.

questions.question: How to create a core dump file in linux?
answer: ulimit -c unlimited
Check the setting:
ulimit -a
The default path where core dumps are stored is then in /var/lib/systemd/coredump.

questions.question: How to compile code for gdb and run?
answer: gcc program -o program.out -g
g flag means you can see the proper names of variables and functions in your stack frames, get line numbers and see the source as you step around in the executable.
gdb ./program.out

questions.question: What are gdb usefull commands?
answer: Here are few useful commands to get started with gdb for the above example:-
run or r : executes the program from start to end.
break or b : sets breakpoint on a particular line.
Info b : see the breakpoint info
disable : disable a breakpoint.
enable : enable a disabled breakpoint.
next or n : executes next line of code, but don’t dive into functions.
step : go to next instruction, diving into the function.
list or l : displays the code.by default first 10 lines.
print or p : used to display the stored value.
quit or q : exits out of gdb.
clear : to clear all breakpoints.
continue : continue normal execution.

questions.question: How to apply GDB to core dump?
questions.code:
gdb program.o -c corefile 

bt full or where

questions.question: How to see the current/number of threads and how to set a particular thread?
answer: (gdb) info threads
output:
3 process 35 thread 27  0x34e5 in sigpause ()
2 process 35 thread 23  0x34e5 in sigpause ()
* 1 process 35 thread 13  main (argc=1, argv=0x7ffffff8)
at threadtest.c:68
Now to set to particular thread:
Thread <thread id>
Example:
questions.code: thread 27

questions.question: What is GDB and how do you prepare a program for debugging?
answer: GDB is the GNU debugger. It lets you pause a running program, look at variables and memory, and step through code line by line.
Compile with -g so the binary carries debug symbols (file names, line numbers, variable names). Use -O0 as well, because optimisation reorders or removes code and makes stepping confusing.
Without -g you can still debug, but you only see assembly and function names, not source lines.
questions.code:
gcc -g -O0 main.c -o main
gdb ./main

questions.question: What are the different ways to start GDB?
answer: gdb ./prog : load a program, then type run.
gdb --args ./prog a b c : load the program with command-line arguments. (Or use 'set args a b c' / 'run a b c' inside gdb.)
gdb -p <pid> : attach to an already running process.
gdb ./prog core : analyse a core dump after a crash.
gdb -batch -ex 'run' -ex 'bt' --args ./prog : run non-interactively, useful in scripts and CI.
questions.code:
gdb --args ./prog input.txt -v
(gdb) run < data.txt        # redirect stdin
(gdb) start                 # temporary breakpoint at main, then run

questions.question: What is the difference between next, step, finish, until and continue?
answer: next (n): run the next line, but treat a function call as one step (does not go inside).
step (s): run the next line and go inside the function if it has debug info.
finish: keep running until the current function returns, then print the return value.
until / advance <line>: run until a line greater than the current one (leaves loops) or until a given location.
continue (c): run until the next breakpoint, signal or exit.
stepi / nexti: the same as step and next, but for one machine instruction.
questions.code:
(gdb) break foo
(gdb) run
(gdb) step      # enter a callee
(gdb) finish    # Run till exit... Value returned is $1 = 42

questions.question: How do you set different kinds of breakpoints?
answer: break func / break file.c:42 : stop at a function or line.
tbreak : temporary breakpoint, deleted after it is hit once.
break file.c:42 if i == 100 : conditional breakpoint.
rbreak ^parse_ : breakpoints on all functions matching a regular expression.
info breakpoints, disable 2, enable 2, delete 2 : manage them.
ignore 1 50 : skip the next 50 hits of breakpoint 1.
questions.code:
(gdb) break loop.c:12 if i == 100
(gdb) condition 1 i == 200     # change condition of breakpoint 1
(gdb) tbreak main

questions.question: What is the difference between a breakpoint and a watchpoint?
answer: A breakpoint stops when execution reaches a certain code location.
A watchpoint stops when the value of a variable or memory address changes, no matter which line changed it. It is the best tool to find 'who overwrote my variable?'.
watch var (on write), rwatch var (on read), awatch var (on read or write).

Hardware watchpoints use CPU debug registers and are fast, but the number is limited (about 4 on x86). When the limit is exceeded, GDB falls back to software watchpoints, which single-step and are very slow.
questions.code:
(gdb) watch counter
(gdb) watch *(int*)0x7ffe1234abcd
(gdb) watch arr[3] if arr[3] > 10

questions.question: How do you find the cause of a segmentation fault using GDB?
answer: Run the program inside gdb. When it crashes, gdb stops at the exact line. Then type bt to see the call chain.
Use 'frame N' to jump to a stack frame, 'info locals' and 'print ptr' to check which pointer is NULL or invalid.
If the crash happened somewhere else (for example on a customer machine), use the core file.
questions.code:
(gdb) run
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
(gdb) bt
(gdb) frame 1
(gdb) info locals
(gdb) print *node

questions.question: How do you debug using a core dump?
answer: A core dump is a snapshot of the process memory at the time of the crash. Enable it with 'ulimit -c unlimited' in the shell before running the program.
Where the file goes depends on /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. On many modern systems it is piped to systemd-coredump, so use coredumpctl gdb instead of looking for a file named core.
Open it with gdb <binary> <core>. The binary must be the same build that crashed, ideally with debug symbols.
questions.code:
ulimit -c unlimited
./prog          # crashes, writes core
gdb ./prog core
(gdb) bt full

questions.question: How do you print variables, arrays, structures and memory in GDB?
answer: print var, print *ptr, print ptr->field, print/x var (hex), print/t var (binary), print/c var (char).
Arrays through a pointer: print *arr@10 prints 10 elements starting at arr. (Plain print arr@10 does not do what you expect.)
x (examine memory): x/<count><format><size> address. For example x/8xb &var shows 8 bytes in hex, x/4dw shows 4 words in decimal, x/s str prints a string, x/5i $pc prints 5 instructions.
ptype shows the full type definition, whatis shows the type name only.
set print pretty on makes structures easy to read.
questions.code:
(gdb) print *arr@5
$1 = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
(gdb) x/8xb &value
(gdb) x/s name
(gdb) ptype struct node
(gdb) set print pretty on

questions.question: How do you change a variable or call a function while debugging?
answer: set var x = 10 changes a variable (print x = 10 also does it).
call func(3) or print func(3) runs a function in the debugged program.
return (with an optional value) pops the current frame and returns immediately, skipping the rest of the function.
jump <line> continues from another line. Be careful, because this can leave the stack in a bad state.
questions.code:
(gdb) set var retries = 0
(gdb) call cleanup(buf)
(gdb) return -1

questions.question: How do you move around the call stack?
answer: backtrace (bt) shows the call stack. bt full also shows local variables of each frame. bt 5 shows only the innermost 5 frames.
frame N selects a frame, up and down move one frame. After selecting a frame, info locals and print show variables of that frame.
info frame gives details like saved registers and return address.

questions.question: How do you debug a multi-threaded program in GDB?
answer: info threads lists all threads. thread N switches to thread N.
thread apply all bt prints the backtrace of every thread. This is the first command for deadlock investigation: look for threads waiting in pthread_mutex_lock.
By default, when you stop at a breakpoint, all threads stop (all-stop mode). When you step, other threads may run too. Use set scheduler-locking on to freeze other threads while stepping.
break foo thread 2 sets a breakpoint only for thread 2.
questions.code:
(gdb) info threads
(gdb) thread apply all bt
(gdb) set scheduler-locking on

questions.question: How do you debug a program that calls fork()?
answer: By default gdb keeps following the parent and the child runs free, so breakpoints in the child are never hit.
set follow-fork-mode child makes gdb follow the child.
set detach-on-fork off keeps both processes under gdb. Then use info inferiors and inferior N to switch.
For exec() use set follow-exec-mode.
questions.code:
(gdb) set follow-fork-mode child
(gdb) set detach-on-fork off
(gdb) break child_work
(gdb) run

questions.question: Why does gdb show '<optimized out>' and why do breakpoints land on strange lines?
answer: The binary was built with optimisation (-O1, -O2, -O3). The compiler may keep a variable only in a register for a short time, merge or reorder lines, and inline functions.
Rebuild with -O0 -g for debugging. If you must debug a release build, use -Og or -O2 -g, and expect jumps in the line order.
Also remember that a bug that disappears at -O0 often means undefined behaviour or a missing volatile.

questions.question: What is the difference between -g, -ggdb and -g3? What if the binary is stripped?
answer: -g produces debug info in the platform's native format (DWARF on Linux). -ggdb produces extra gdb-specific info. -g3 also includes macro definitions, so you can print macros.

A stripped binary has no symbols, so bt shows only addresses. You can keep the debug info in a separate file with objcopy --only-keep-debug and load it in gdb using symbol-file or by build-id. Many distributions provide debuginfod to download symbols automatically.
questions.code:
objcopy --only-keep-debug prog prog.debug
strip prog
gdb -s prog.debug -e prog

questions.question: How do you attach gdb to a running process and why can 'Operation not permitted' happen?
answer: Use gdb -p <pid> or attach <pid> inside gdb. The process is paused when you attach. detach lets it continue.
On many Linux systems, ptrace is restricted by Yama: /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope = 1 allows attaching only to your own child processes. Either run as root (sudo gdb -p pid) or set it to 0.
In containers, ptrace needs the SYS_PTRACE capability.
questions.code:
sudo gdb -p $(pidof myserver)
(gdb) thread apply all bt
(gdb) detach

questions.question: What is remote debugging with gdbserver?
answer: gdbserver runs on the target (for example an embedded board) and controls the program. gdb runs on your development PC and connects over TCP or serial.
The PC copy of the binary has the symbols, so the target can have a small stripped binary. Use a cross-gdb (for example arm-none-eabi-gdb or aarch64-linux-gnu-gdb) matching the target.
questions.code:
# on target
gdbserver :1234 ./app
# on host
gdb-multiarch ./app
(gdb) target remote 192.168.1.10:1234

questions.question: How do you handle signals in gdb?
answer: gdb stops when the program receives many signals. Use handle SIGUSR1 nostop noprint pass so gdb does not stop but still delivers the signal to the program.
info signals lists the settings.
You can send a signal yourself with signal SIGINT, or discard it with signal 0.
questions.code:
(gdb) handle SIGALRM nostop noprint pass
(gdb) handle SIGPIPE stop print

questions.question: How can you stop a hung or infinite-loop program in gdb and find where it is stuck?
answer: Press Ctrl+C in gdb. It sends SIGINT and the program stops where it is. Then use bt, and step a few times.
For a program that is not under gdb, attach with gdb -p and run thread apply all bt.
Do this a few times: if the same function appears every time, that is where it spends its time or waits.

questions.question: How do you automate actions at a breakpoint (commands, logging, .gdbinit)?
answer: The commands block runs gdb commands when a breakpoint is hit, for example print a variable and continue. This works like adding a printf without recompiling.
dprintf location,"format",args is a shortcut that prints and continues.
Put settings in ~/.gdbinit (global) or .gdbinit (project, needs auto-load permission). Run scripts with gdb -x script.gdb.
questions.code:
(gdb) break process if id > 100
(gdb) commands
> silent
> printf "id=%d\n", id
> continue
> end
(gdb) dprintf file.c:50,"x=%d\n", x

questions.question: What is reverse debugging in gdb?
answer: With record (record full), gdb saves each step so you can run backwards using reverse-next, reverse-step, reverse-continue and reverse-finish. It is slow and uses a lot of memory, but it is very helpful to find where a value became wrong.
Tools like rr give a faster and more reliable record and replay for Linux.
questions.code:
(gdb) break main
(gdb) run
(gdb) record
(gdb) continue
(gdb) reverse-continue

questions.question: How do you look at registers, assembly and the instruction pointer?
answer: info registers (or info registers rip) shows CPU registers. p $rsp, p $pc also work.
disassemble shows the assembly of the current function. disassemble /s mixes source and assembly.
x/10i $pc shows the next 10 instructions. layout asm or layout split shows them in the TUI.
set disassembly-flavor intel gives Intel syntax instead of AT&T.

questions.question: Why is my breakpoint not hit or shown as 'pending'?
answer: Common causes: no debug info (-g missing), the code is in a shared library not loaded yet (gdb asks to make the breakpoint pending; use set breakpoint pending on), the line has no code because of optimisation, a different binary is being run than the source you are looking at, or the function was inlined.
Check with info breakpoints, info sharedlibrary and info source. Also check that the source path is right (directory command or set substitute-path).

questions.question: What is TUI mode?
answer: A text user interface inside the terminal that shows the source code in a window above the gdb prompt. Start with gdb -tui, or press Ctrl+X A to toggle. layout src, layout asm, layout regs, layout split pick the windows.
If the screen gets garbled use Ctrl+L to refresh.

questions.question: How do you debug a stack overflow or a corrupted stack?
answer: A stack overflow from deep recursion shows a very long backtrace (bt -20 shows the outermost 20 frames, bt 20 the innermost). Look for a repeating function pattern.

For a corrupted stack (return address overwritten), the backtrace is garbage or ends at 0x4141414141. Use a watchpoint on the buffer neighbour or build with -fstack-protector or AddressSanitizer to find the overflowing write.
Check the stack limit with ulimit -s.

questions.question: Can you step into a function that has no debug info, and why does 'step' skip it?
answer: step does not enter functions that have no line info (like libc functions) and acts like next. Use stepi to go instruction by instruction, or set step-mode on so step also enters such functions at the assembly level.
To skip uninteresting functions deliberately, use skip function foo or skip file bar.c.
questions.code:
(gdb) skip function std::vector<int>::operator[]
(gdb) set step-mode on

topics.title: Valgrind
topics.description: Memory error and leak detection, profiling and thread checking.

questions.question: How will you find memory leaks?
answer: Memory leak occurs when programmers create a memory in heap and forget to delete it.
Valgrind\
--tool=memcheck(fine grained memory checker)/massif(measures how much heap memory prog uses)/cachegrind(cache simulator)  \
--leak-check=full \
--show-leak-kinds=all \
--track-origins=yes \
--verbose \
--log-file=valgrind-out.txt \
./executable exampleParam1
questions.code: valgrind --tool=memcheck --leak-check=full MyProgram.out

questions.question: What is Valgrind and which tools does it have?
answer: Valgrind is a framework that runs your program on a virtual CPU and instruments it to find problems, without recompiling. Its tools are:
Memcheck (default): memory errors and leaks.
Helgrind and DRD: data races and lock-order problems in threads.
Massif: heap usage over time. DHAT: heap allocation behaviour.
Cachegrind: cache and branch prediction simulation. Callgrind: call graph profile (view with KCachegrind).
Choose a tool with --tool=<name>.
questions.code:
valgrind ./prog                  # memcheck by default
valgrind --tool=helgrind ./prog

questions.question: How do you run Valgrind to get the most useful report?
answer: Compile with -g (and -O0 or -O1) so the report has file names and line numbers.
Use --leak-check=full to see where each leak was allocated, --show-leak-kinds=all to include all kinds, and --track-origins=yes to learn where an uninitialised value came from (slower).
--error-exitcode=1 makes Valgrind return a failure code, so it is useful in CI.
questions.code:
gcc -g -O0 main.c -o main
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
         --track-origins=yes --error-exitcode=1 ./main

questions.question: What are the leak categories: definitely lost, indirectly lost, possibly lost and still reachable?
answer: Definitely lost: no pointer to the block exists anymore. A real leak. Fix it first.
Indirectly lost: the block is only reachable from a block that is definitely lost (for example nodes of a list whose head was lost). Fixing the parent fixes these.
Possibly lost: only a pointer into the middle of the block exists. It may be a leak, or you may be using interior pointers on purpose.

Still reachable: a pointer still exists at exit (for example a global), but the memory was not freed. It is not a leak in the sense of growing memory, and many programs do this on purpose, but it can hide problems in long-running programs.

questions.question: What are the common error messages Memcheck prints and what do they mean?
answer: Invalid read / write of size N: access outside an allocated block, or to freed memory (use-after-free). The message says how far from a block it was, for example '4 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd'.
Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s): an if/loop used a variable that was never set.
Invalid free() / delete: freeing a pointer twice, or a pointer that did not come from malloc.
Mismatched free() / delete / delete []: allocated with one family (malloc, new, new[]) and released with another.
Source and destination overlap in memcpy: should use memmove.
Syscall param write(buf) points to uninitialised byte(s): writing garbage to a file or socket (can leak secrets).

questions.question: How does Valgrind (Memcheck) work and what is its cost?
answer: It uses dynamic binary instrumentation: it translates your machine code on the fly and adds checking code. It replaces malloc/free with its own versions to track each block, and keeps shadow memory that records which bytes are addressable and which bits are initialised.
Cost: programs run roughly 10 to 50 times slower and use more memory. So use small test inputs, or run in nightly tests.

questions.question: What can Valgrind NOT detect?
answer: It does not reliably detect overflow of arrays on the stack or in global/static memory, because it only knows the bounds of heap blocks. An overflow inside a struct, or from one stack variable into its neighbour, is also missed.
It only finds problems on paths that your test actually executes.
It cannot find logic errors, and it is not meant for finding data races with Memcheck (use Helgrind or DRD).
For stack and global overflows use AddressSanitizer.

questions.question: Valgrind vs AddressSanitizer (ASan): when do you use which?
answer: ASan is built into the compiler (-fsanitize=address). It needs a rebuild, but is only about 2x slower, and it detects stack, global and heap overflows and use-after-return. LeakSanitizer is included on Linux.
Valgrind needs no rebuild and works on any binary (including third-party libraries), and detects uninitialised value use, which ASan does not (that is MemorySanitizer).
Do not use both at the same time in the same process. In practice: run ASan day to day, and use Valgrind when you cannot rebuild or need uninitialised-memory checks.
questions.code: gcc -g -fsanitize=address,undefined main.c -o main_asan

questions.question: Is 'total heap usage: 10 allocs, 10 frees' proof that there are no leaks?
answer: Not by itself. The counts only say the number of calls, not that each free matched the right block. A double free plus a missing free can still show equal counts.
The reliable line is 'All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible'. Read the full leak summary and the error summary too.

questions.question: How do you find the origin of 'Conditional jump depends on uninitialised value'?
answer: Run with --track-origins=yes. Valgrind then adds 'Uninitialised value was created by a heap allocation / stack allocation at ...' with a stack trace.

Remember that the error is reported where the value is USED in a decision, not where it was left uninitialised. Valgrind allows copying uninitialised values around silently and complains only at a branch, an address use or a system call.

questions.question: Why does Valgrind show no line numbers or '???' in the stack trace?
answer: The program (or the library) was built without -g, or it was stripped. Rebuild with -g. For system libraries install their debug symbol packages.
High optimisation can also give confusing line numbers, so use -O0 or -O1.

questions.question: How do you use suppressions?
answer: A suppression file hides known, harmless errors, usually from third-party or system libraries that you cannot fix.
Run with --gen-suppressions=all to print a ready-made suppression block after each error, copy the ones you want to a file, and pass --suppressions=my.supp.
Use them carefully, so you do not hide real bugs.
questions.code:
valgrind --gen-suppressions=all ./prog 2> out.txt
valgrind --suppressions=my.supp ./prog

questions.question: How do you detect data races and deadlocks with Valgrind?
answer: Use Helgrind (--tool=helgrind) or DRD (--tool=drd). Both watch pthread calls and memory accesses. Helgrind reports 'Possible data race during read/write' when two threads access the same location without a common lock, and also reports lock-order violations that can lead to deadlock.
They are slower than Memcheck and may give false positives with custom synchronisation (such as lock-free code) unless annotated.
questions.code: valgrind --tool=helgrind ./threaded_prog

questions.question: How do you profile heap usage with Massif?
answer: valgrind --tool=massif ./prog writes massif.out.<pid>. Read it with ms_print massif.out.<pid>, which shows a graph of heap size over time and the allocation call chains at peak usage.
Use --time-unit=B to measure time in bytes allocated and --pages-as-heap=yes to include all memory pages (not only malloc).
questions.code:
valgrind --tool=massif ./prog
ms_print massif.out.12345 | less

questions.question: How do you find slow functions with Callgrind and Cachegrind?
answer: valgrind --tool=callgrind ./prog creates callgrind.out.<pid>. View it with kcachegrind or callgrind_annotate. It shows instruction counts per function and per call, which is deterministic (not affected by machine noise).
Cachegrind (--tool=cachegrind) simulates caches and branches, and shows cache misses per line with cg_annotate.
questions.code:
valgrind --tool=callgrind ./prog
callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.12345

questions.question: How do you use Valgrind with a program that forks or has multiple processes?
answer: By default Valgrind only follows the main process. Use --trace-children=yes to also follow child processes started by fork and exec.
Use --log-file=vg.%p.log so each process writes to its own file (%p is the pid).
questions.code: valgrind --trace-children=yes --log-file=vg.%p.log ./launcher

questions.question: How can you combine Valgrind with GDB?
answer: Start with --vgdb=yes --vgdb-error=0. Valgrind stops at startup and waits for a gdb connection. In gdb run target remote | vgdb. You can then continue and gdb stops at the first Valgrind error, where you can inspect variables.
Inside gdb you can also use monitor commands such as monitor leak_check full.
questions.code:
valgrind --vgdb=yes --vgdb-error=0 ./prog
# other terminal
gdb ./prog
(gdb) target remote | vgdb

questions.question: Why does Valgrind report leaks in memory I free at exit, or errors in libc?
answer: Many libraries allocate memory that lives until exit (still reachable), which is normal. Also some libraries, like OpenSSL or glibc, trigger known false positives, which distributions ship suppression files for.
If you free memory inside an atexit handler, the leak check runs after the handlers, so it is fine.

questions.question: Why does a program behave differently (or not crash) under Valgrind?
answer: Valgrind changes timing (so races can disappear), memory layout (uninitialised memory is filled with different bytes), and it makes malloc return memory at different addresses.
A bug that vanishes under Valgrind, or only appears there, often means undefined behaviour or a race. Try Helgrind, ASan and TSan as well.

questions.question: What are Valgrind's limits on platforms and static binaries?
answer: Valgrind supports Linux on x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64, PPC, MIPS, s390x, and some other platforms. Support for macOS on newer versions is limited or missing, and Windows is not supported (use tools like Dr. Memory or the compiler sanitizers).
Statically linked executables are a problem, because Valgrind cannot replace malloc inside them, so memory errors are mostly not detected. Link dynamically when testing.
